results.title: Teleportation-Based Continuous Variable Quantum Cryptography
results.description:
# Teleportation-Based Continuous Variable Quantum Cryptography
###### Abstract
We present a continuous variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) scheme based on the CV quantum teleportation of coherent states that yields a raw secret key made up of discrete variables for both Alice and Bob. This protocol preserves the efficient detection schemes of current CV technology (no single-photon detection techniques) and, at the same time, has efficient error correction and privacy amplification schemes due to the binary modulation of the key ## 1 Introduction
Since this protocol works deterministically (no postselection) and uses a discrete modulation for the key, it achieves fairly high key rates over long distances, even assuming the usual conservative reconciliation efficiencies for CV protocols based on binary modulated keys Lev09. Apart from its possible practical significance, this protocol also adds to our fundamental understanding of CVQKD since it is based on the active use of CV teleportation protocols Bra98, opening up alternative ways to understand the security of CVQKD as well as different routes for future unconditional security proofs Following Gor10; Lui14, the main idea behind the present teleportation-based CVQKD scheme is the active use of the finite resources (finite squeezing) inherently associated to the CV teleportation protocol, combined with the knowledge of the pool of coherent states with Alice to be teleported to Bob Lui14. It is by properly making use of these two pieces of information that we can build a protocol furnishing high key rates even in a scenario with high losses, turning the finiteness of squeezing into an advantage ## 2 The protocol
The present teleportation-based CVQKD protocol works as follows. Alice divides her pool of coherent states into two sets, {|α⟩,|−α⟩}\{|\alpha\rangle,|-\alpha\rangle\} and {|iα⟩,|−iα⟩}\{|i\alpha\rangle,|-i\alpha\rangle\}, which we respectively call real and imaginary basis (α>0\alpha>0) As mentioned above, a key feature of the present protocol is the fact that the optimal (gu,gv)(g_{u},g_{v}) can be chosen such that they do not depend on the sign of the teleported coherent state, depending only on the state being real or imaginary. We can see that this can be done by looking at the functional form of FF after a single run of the protocol. Assuming, for definiteness, we are dealing with real coherent states we have ## 4 Conclusion
In summary, we proposed a new and efficient CVQKD scheme with a binary encoding for the key (discrete modulation) based on the CV teleportation of coherent states, where the CV teleportation protocol is not just a substitute to the direct sending of coherent states from Alice to Bob for the usual CVQKD protocols We showed that the present teleportation-based CVQKD protocol is secure against individual attacks and in particular that it works with direct reconciliation and no postselection even for very high loss in the optical channel connecting Alice and Bob. Moreover, we showed that it is possible to achieve fairly high key rates with mild squeezing (≈2\approx 2 dB) near the 100%100\% loss regime. This fact combined with the high repetition rates of CV technology may lead to efficient long distance QKD protocols ## Appendix B The teleportation-based CVQKD protocol
The present CVQKD protocol is based on a binary encoding for the key such that {|−α⟩,|α⟩,|−iα⟩,|iα⟩}={0,1,0,1}\{|-\alpha\rangle,|\alpha\rangle,|-i\alpha\rangle,|i\alpha\rangle\}=\{0,1,0,1\}, with α\alpha a real number. These states are to be teleported from Alice to Bob randomly Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF
Abstract 1 Introduction 2 The protocol 3 Security analysis 4 Conclusion A The modified CV teleportation protocol B The teleportation-based CVQKD protocol B.1 Fidelity analysis B.2 Key generation analysis C Security analysis C.1 Lossy channel or the presence of Eve C.2 Secure key rates D Further examples References

# Plan talk (no prompts yet, no code yet)

You answered the grill. Here’s the locked picture, the tension in your answers, and a plan that can still **win SIH 26141** without lying about physics.

---

## 1. What you actually decided

| Topic | Your call | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Success | **Everything** (demo + metrics + infra feel) | We phase it or we die |
| Judges | Unpredictable → serve **both** | Flash demo + hard numbers |
| Quantum honesty | Sim **and** real API path | Aer/default + optional IBM/cloud backend |
| Repo | **Same GitHub** ShorlyNot | Evolve product, don’t abandon brand |
| Extra security | **QKD + PQC** beside QDS | Hybrid platform story |
| Time | “Make it better *NOW*” | Ruthless MVP first |
| Team | **Solo** + agentic IDEs | I write prompts; you run; I review GitHub |
| PS constraints | All locked, **no ML** | Thresholds only |
| Protocol | Papers + **novelty** | Cite base, add detection framework |
| Sign modes | User **chooses** signature kind | Pluggable sign profiles |
| Parties | Signer + Verifier + **Arbiter** | AQS-style |
| Noise | Realistic + extra on real API | Two noise layers |
| Stack | **Qiskit + PennyLane** + pro UI | Dual backend |
| Product | **Platform/infra**, not a toy page | Apps + packages layout |
| Name | **ShorlyNot** | Keep |
| Claims | Only what we truly have | No “unbreakable” |
| Process | **Plan now → prompts later** | This message |

---

## 2. Honest tension (don’t skip this)

You asked for:

- full PS fit  
- novelty beyond papers  
- QDS + QKD + PQC  
- Qiskit + PennyLane  
- real quantum API  
- arbiter  
- multi signature modes  
- professional platform UI  
- all metrics  
- solo, right now  

That’s **3 products**. Solo + “now” means we **sequence**, not shrink the dream to zero.

**Rule that wins SIH:**

> **Phase 1 = PS 26141 complete and demoable.**  
> **Phase 2 = platform (QKD/PQC/UI polish).**  
> **Phase 3 = real QPU + extra novelty.**  

If Phase 1 isn’t solid, Phase 2 is lipstick on the wrong pig (your old QKD-only state).

---

## 3. Product one-liner (pitch)

**ShorlyNot** becomes:

> A quantum-security **platform** whose core for SIH 26141 is a **teleportation-based Quantum Digital Signature** service with a **non-ML, measurement-statistic threat engine** (forgery / impersonation / replay / unauthorized verify / channel manip), optionally wrapped with **QKD session keys** and **PQC-protected classical correction channels**.

Old BB84 chat/router stuff = **legacy modules** under the same brand, not the hero.

---

## 4. Research base (real citations) + where novelty sits

### Papers we stand on (implement / cite)

**Teleportation & Pauli corrections (foundation)**  
1. Bennett et al., *Teleporting an unknown quantum state…*, Phys. Rev. Lett. 70, 1895 (1993). (canonical teleportation + Pauli corrections)

**Quantum digital signatures (classic QDS line)**  
2. Gottesman & Chuang, *Quantum Digital Signatures*, [arXiv:quant-ph/0105032](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0105032)

**Arbitrated / teleportation-linked signature schemes (matches your Q13 = arbiter)**  
3. Lu, Li, Yu, Han, *A Verifiable Arbitrated Quantum Signature Scheme Based on Controlled Quantum Teleportation*, Entropy 24(1):111 (2022). ([MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/1099-4300/24/1/111) / five-qubit controlled teleportation AQS)  
4. Luo et al., *Two Quantum Proxy Blind Signature Schemes Based on Controlled Quantum Teleportation*, [arXiv:2210.14438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14438)  
5. Zheng, Chang, Zhang, *Arbitrated quantum signature with quantum teleportation using GHZ…* (QIP 2020 line; GHZ teleportation AQS)

**Forgery / Pauli attack reality (why detection matters)**  
6. Gao et al. / follow-ons on **Pauli forgery** in AQS (QOTP commuting with Paulis) — see discussion in [arXiv:1407.1380](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1380) and newer encryption fixes e.g. controlled-unitary AQS [arXiv:2507.10233](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.10233)  
7. Recent cryptanalysis of teleportation-AQS: *Cryptanalysis of four arbitrated quantum signature schemes*, [arXiv HTML 2603.19985](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19985) (shows Lu-style controlled teleportation AQS can still be forged under some models)

**QKD-assisted / hybrid signature thinking**  
8. *Generalized Quantum-assisted Digital Signature (GQaDS)*, [arXiv:2406.19978](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19978) — QKD keys + forgery/repudiation probability tradeoffs  
9. Counterfactual / twin-field QDS: [arXiv:2310.11308](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11308)

**Protect classical teleportation bits with PQC (your QKD+PQC instinct, modern)**  
10. *Quantum-Resistant Quantum Teleportation (QRQT)*, [arXiv:2604.16101](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.16101v1) — PQC on Pauli correction bits \(M_1,M_2\)

**Measurement / fidelity stats toolkit**  
11. Flammia & Liu, *Direct Fidelity Estimation from Few Pauli Measurements*, [arXiv:1104.4695](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.4695)

We **do not** re-implement every paper. We pick a **simplified controlled-teleportation AQS core** (inspired by 3 + Bennett), and put novelty in the **threat layer**.

### Novelty (this is “better than just papers”)

Papers give **protocols**. PS wants a **threat detection framework**. Novelty stack:

1. **Q-STDF — Quantum Signature Threat Detection Framework**  
   Unified engine: same feature vector from verify transcript → threshold rules → threat label.  
   Features: mismatch rate, Pauli-basis histogram divergence, nonce reuse, key-binding fail, correction-bit integrity, unauthorized verify, optional timing.

2. **Multi-profile signatures (your Q12)**  
   User selects mode:  
   - `QDS-TELEPORT` (hero, PS)  
   - `QDS-AQS-ARBITER` (Trent path)  
   - `HYBRID-QKD-MAC` (GQaDS-inspired, classical MAC with QKD key — *not* a substitute for QDS)  
   - `PQC-CLASSICAL` (Dilithium/ML-DSA style contrast — shows “post-quantum classical” vs “quantum signature”)  
   Platform switch; demo default = teleport QDS.

3. **Hybrid classical path (QRQT-inspired)**  
   Teleportation correction bits protected by **PQC KEM + AEAD** (you already have ML-KEM ideas in ShorlyNot). Attack toggle: strip PQC → channel manip succeeds more.

4. **Dual engine: Qiskit + PennyLane**  
   Same protocol, two circuit backends, cross-check metrics (consistency = trust story for judges).

5. **Real-device noise adapter**  
   Sim noise model + when IBM/cloud API used, fold **backend-reported** noise/errors into thresholds (adaptive τ), not fake fixed QBER.

6. **Forgery probability lab**  
   Monte Carlo + analytical bound display (Hoeffding on mismatch counts), attack grid, exportable metrics — evaluation module PS asks for.

**Claim carefully:** novelty is the **framework + hybrid ops + dual-backend evaluation**, not “we invented teleportation.”

---

## 5. Architecture (combine with current repo)

Evolve **one** platform under `shorlynot/` (clean), keep old trees as `legacy/` or stop advertising them.

```text
shorlynot/
  packages/
    qds/           # NEW hero — teleport AQS sign/verify
      profiles/    # teleport | arbiter | ...
      circuit/     # qiskit_backend.py, pennylane_backend.py
    detect/        # NEW — Q-STDF thresholds (no ML)
    attacks/       # NEW — forge/replay/impersonate/unauth/channel
    analysis/      # NEW — P_forge, ROC-ish rates, latency
    qkd/           # EXISTING bb84/e91… keep as module
    pqc/           # EXISTING mlkem — wire to correction channel
    crypto/        # leases etc. demoted
    common/
  apps/
    control_plane/ # API: sign/verify/attack/metrics/backends
    threat_console/# attacker + SOC style UI
    dashboard/     # platform UI (signature pipeline + SOC + bank story)
    legacy_chat/   # old demo optional
  docs/
    MODEL.md
    REFERENCES.md
    DELIVERY_TABLE.md
    SPEC.md
    DEMO_SCRIPT.md
  tests/
```

**Judge entrypoint:** one command → API + dashboard focused on **QDS + threats**.  
QKD/PQC visible as **platform layers**, not the only story.

---

## 6. Core protocol (Phase 1 — what we implement)

**Roles:** Alice (signer), Bob (verifier), Trent (arbiter) — matches Q13.

**Flow (simplified controlled-teleportation QDS, sim-faithful):**

1. **Setup:** entangled resource distributed (Bell/GHZ-style as profile dictates); key material IDs bound to parties.  
2. **Sign:** message → bit/block encoding into Pauli eigenstates; Alice does Bell measurement / teleportation steps; produces signature transcript (quantum outcomes + classical Pauli bits + nonce + key_id + profile).  
3. **Classical path:** correction bits optionally wrapped with **PQC** (QRQT-inspired).  
4. **Verify:** Bob (+ Trent if arbiter mode) applies Pauli corrections, projective measurements, compares to expected; compute mismatch stats.  
5. **Detect (Q-STDF):** threshold rules → `OK | FORGERY | REPLAY | IMPERSONATION | UNAUTH_VERIFY | CHANNEL`.  
6. **Analyze:** log metrics for the evaluation suite.

**Legit path:** accept with high probability under declared noise; ideal channel → deterministic accept.  
**Forge path:** random/Pauli-tampered sig → reject + high detect rate.  
We document known paper attacks (Gao/Lu cryptanalysis) and show **detector catches the sim versions**.

---

## 7. Detection design (your “all features” + τ)

**τ (threshold):**  
Not magic. For mismatch count \(X\) over \(n\) checked qubits, under honest noise \(p_0\):

\[
\tau = p_0 + \epsilon,\quad \epsilon \sim \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}
\]

(Hoeffding-style; show formula in UI).  
Presets: **strict / normal / lenient** (your Q20 = show both error types).

**Feature pack (Q17 all + extras):**

| Feature | Threat |
|---|---|
| Mismatch rate > τ | forgery / channel |
| Pauli histogram divergence | forgery / wrong encoding |
| Nonce / sig_id reuse | replay |
| key_id / share binding fail | impersonation |
| Verify without entitlement | unauthorized verification |
| Correction MAC/PQC fail or bit flips | channel manip |
| **Novelty:** cross-backend disagree (Qiskit vs PennyLane) | implementation/channel anomaly |
| **Novelty:** adaptive τ shift when real-API noise rises | device-aware detection |

**No sklearn, no torch.** Ever.

---

## 8. Phased delivery (solo + NOW)

### Phase 1 — **PS win pack** (do first, no excuses)

1. `packages/qds` teleport sign/verify (Qiskit Aer)  
2. Arbiter mode flag  
3. `packages/detect` Q-STDF  
4. `packages/attacks` five attacks from PS  
5. `packages/analysis` P_forge + rates + latency  
6. FastAPI control plane  
7. pytest suite  
8. docs: MODEL, REFERENCES, DELIVERY_TABLE, SPEC  
9. Minimal but **pro** dashboard page: pipeline + threats + metrics  

**Exit criteria:** outsider runs README, sees legit green, four attacks red, numbers match PS language.

### Phase 2 — **Platform**

1. Wire existing QKD module as session/key service  
2. Wire PQC on classical correction channel  
3. Signature profile switcher  
4. PennyLane backend parity  
5. Richer dashboard (SOC feed + banking message + pipeline)  
6. Fold/hide legacy duplicates in repo story  

### Phase 3 — **Stretch**

1. Real IBM Quantum (or compatible) backend switch  
2. Device noise → adaptive τ  
3. Extra profiles (proxy/blind **stub** only if time)  
4. Demo video / synthetic dataset export  

---

## 9. What we promise in claims (Q36)

**Say:**  
- Simulation of teleportation-based QDS with information-theoretic *motivation* under stated model  
- Threshold detection with measured forge/false-accept rates in sim  
- Optional PQC on classical bits; optional QKD subsystem  
- Optional real-backend path when credentials exist  

**Don’t say:**  
- Production ITS on the internet today  
- “Unforgeable under all attacks”  
- ML-free as if that alone is the invention  

---

## 10. How you + I work (Q44)

```text
me:  SPEC + ordered prompts (copy into your agentic IDE)
you: run prompt → commit → push GitHub
me:  pull/review repo → gap list → next prompt
```

No giant one-shot “build everything” prompt.  
**Prompt batches = Phase 1 slices** (ponytail: one vertical slice that runs).

---

## 11. Risks I’m not sugarcoating

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Scope explosion | Phase 1 freeze list |
| Dual Qiskit+PennyLane delays core | Qiskit first, PennyLane interface stub day 1, fill Phase 2 |
| Real QPU flaky/slow | always Aer default; real is toggle |
| Paper protocols too heavy | simplified AQS; cite full papers |
| Old monorepo mess confuses judges | single README path: “SIH 26141 → shorlynot QDS” |
| Novelty overclaim | novelty = Q-STDF + hybrid + dual-backend eval |

---

## 12. Freeze list (Phase 1)

**Out until Phase 1 green:**

- OpenWrt/iptables as main demo  
- ML baselines  
- Full blind/proxy multiparty as real crypto  
- Merging every duplicate folder  
- Mobile app  
- Perfect literature clone of 6-qubit proxy blind schemes  

**In Phase 1:**

- Teleport QDS + arbiter  
- Pauli/projective/threshold detect  
- 5 attack classes PS named  
- Forgery probability + performance metrics  
- Pro-enough UI + API  
- References.md with real arXiv  

---

## 13. Success checklist (map to PS objectives)

| PS objective | Our artifact |
|---|---|
| Framework for teleportation-based QDS | `packages/qds` + `detect` |
| Detect forgery, impersonation, replay, unauth verify | `attacks` + `detect` labels |
| Pauli eigenstates, measurement analysis, statistical thresholds | encode + verify + τ engine |
| Efficient verify, ITS framing | complexity notes + model doc |
| Forgery prob, attack sims, performance | `analysis` + dashboard |

---

## 14. Decision I need from you before prompts

Reply with **YES** to this frozen plan, or edit bullets:

1. **Phase 1 first** (PS core), platform candy after — **locked?**  
2. Hero protocol = **simplified controlled-teleportation AQS** (Lu/Bennett-inspired), novelty in **Q-STDF** — **locked?**  
3. Repo work lives under **`shorlynot/`** on existing GitHub — **locked?**  
4. Backends: **Qiskit Aer mandatory in P1**; PennyLane **interface + one parity test in P1**, full parity P2 — **locked?**  
5. QKD + PQC = **P2 wiring**, thin hooks in P1 only — **locked?**  
6. Next step after YES = I write **`docs/SPEC.md` outline** in chat, then **Prompt 0 (repo layout + SPEC file)** for your IDE — **locked?**

If you say **`all locked`**, next message is the full plan summary + first prompt batch structure (still plan-ish), then Prompt 0.

If you want changes (e.g. “PennyLane full in P1” or “QKD in P1”), say which number to flip.

---

**Bottom line:**  
Your answers point to a **ShorlyNot quantum security platform**.  
SIH grades **QDS threat detection**.  
Plan = make the platform **true**, but **ship the PS heart first**, with real papers, honest claims, and novelty in the detector—not in pretending the old QKD chat was enough.

"""QTEL frame parser for Arduino optical telemetry.

Parses newline-delimited frames in format:
    QTEL,version,sequence,timestamp_ms,detector_raw,alice_basis,alice_bit,bob_basis,eve_flag,crc

PRD §19.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

from apps.arduino_bridge.crc import validate_frame_crc
from packages.common.errors import SerialCRCFailedError, SerialFrameInvalidError


@dataclass
class QTELFrame:
    """Parsed QTEL telemetry frame."""

    version: int
    sequence: int
    timestamp_ms: int
    detector_raw: int
    alice_basis: int
    alice_bit: int
    bob_basis: int
    eve_flag: int
    crc_valid: bool
    raw_line: str


def parse_qtel_frame(line: str) -> QTELFrame:
    """Parse a single QTEL frame line.

    Args:
        line: Raw line from serial port.

    Returns:
        Parsed QTELFrame.

    Raises:
        SerialFrameInvalidError: If the frame is malformed.
        SerialCRCFailedError: If CRC validation fails.
    """
    line = line.strip()
    if not line:
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError("Empty frame")

    parts = line.split(",")
    if len(parts) != 10:
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(
            f"Expected 10 comma-separated fields, got {len(parts)}: {line}"
        )

    # Validate header
    if parts[0] != "QTEL":
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Invalid header: expected 'QTEL', got '{parts[0]}'")

    try:
        version = int(parts[1])
        sequence = int(parts[2])
        timestamp_ms = int(parts[3])
        detector_raw = int(parts[4])
        alice_basis = int(parts[5])
        alice_bit = int(parts[6])
        bob_basis = int(parts[7])
        eve_flag = int(parts[8])
        crc_value = int(parts[9])
    except ValueError as e:
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Non-integer field in frame: {e}")

    # Validate field ranges
    if version != 1:
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Unsupported protocol version: {version}")

    if alice_basis not in (0, 1):
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Invalid alice_basis: {alice_basis}")

    if alice_bit not in (0, 1):
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Invalid alice_bit: {alice_bit}")

    if bob_basis not in (0, 1):
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Invalid bob_basis: {bob_basis}")

    if eve_flag not in (0, 1):
        raise SerialFrameInvalidError(f"Invalid eve_flag: {eve_flag}")

    # CRC validation
    crc_valid = validate_frame_crc(line)
    if not crc_valid:
        raise SerialCRCFailedError(f"CRC mismatch for frame seq={sequence}")

    return QTELFrame(
        version=version,
        sequence=sequence,
        timestamp_ms=timestamp_ms,
        detector_raw=detector_raw,
        alice_basis=alice_basis,
        alice_bit=alice_bit,
        bob_basis=bob_basis,
        eve_flag=eve_flag,
        crc_valid=crc_valid,
        raw_line=line,
    )


def normalize_intensity(
    raw_value: int,
    dark_level: int,
    bright_level: int,
) -> float:
    """Normalize detector value to [0, 1] range.

    Args:
        raw_value: Raw ADC reading from detector.
        dark_level: Calibrated dark reference.
        bright_level: Calibrated bright reference.

    Returns:
        Normalized intensity clamped to [0, 1].

    Raises:
        CalibrationInvalidError: If bright_level <= dark_level.
    """
    from packages.common.errors import CalibrationInvalidError

    if bright_level <= dark_level:
        raise CalibrationInvalidError(
            f"bright_level ({bright_level}) must exceed dark_level ({dark_level})"
        )

    normalized = (raw_value - dark_level) / (bright_level - dark_level)
    return max(0.0, min(1.0, normalized))

"""CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE implementation for Arduino telemetry frames.

PRD §19: Frame format:
    QTEL,version,sequence,timestamp_ms,detector_raw,alice_basis,alice_bit,bob_basis,eve_flag,crc
"""

from __future__ import annotations


def crc16_ccitt_false(data: bytes, initial: int = 0xFFFF) -> int:
    """Calculate CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE.

    Polynomial: 0x1021
    Initial value: 0xFFFF
    Final XOR: 0x0000
    """
    crc = initial
    for byte in data:
        crc ^= byte << 8
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 0x8000:
                crc = (crc << 1) ^ 0x1021
            else:
                crc = crc << 1
            crc &= 0xFFFF
    return crc


def compute_frame_crc(frame_data: str) -> int:
    """Compute CRC for the data portion of a QTEL frame.

    The CRC covers everything before the last comma-separated CRC field.
    """
    # Everything up to (not including) the final ,<CRC>
    parts = frame_data.strip().rsplit(",", 1)
    if len(parts) != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Cannot split frame for CRC: {frame_data}")

    payload = parts[0]
    return crc16_ccitt_false(payload.encode("ascii"))


def validate_frame_crc(frame_data: str) -> bool:
    """Validate the CRC of a complete QTEL frame.

    Returns True if the embedded CRC matches the computed CRC.
    """
    parts = frame_data.strip().rsplit(",", 1)
    if len(parts) != 2:
        return False

    try:
        embedded_crc = int(parts[1])
    except ValueError:
        return False

    computed = crc16_ccitt_false(parts[0].encode("ascii"))
    return embedded_crc == computed

"""Optical telemetry anomaly detection engine.

Uses rolling windows to detect anomalies in optical channel data.
This is labelled as an OPTICAL QKD PRINCIPLE DEMONSTRATOR, NOT
a true single-photon QKD device.

PRD §20.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

import numpy as np


@dataclass
class AnomalyReport:
    """Report from the optical anomaly detector."""

    window_size: int = 0
    valid_frames: int = 0
    intensity_mean: float = 0.0
    intensity_std: float = 0.0
    bit_disagreement_rate: float = 0.0
    basis_matched_disagreement_rate: float = 0.0
    frame_loss_rate: float = 0.0
    sequence_gaps: int = 0
    anomaly_detected: bool = False
    anomaly_reasons: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    # Label: OPTICAL QKD PRINCIPLE DEMONSTRATOR
    demonstrator_type: str = "OPTICAL QKD PRINCIPLE DEMONSTRATOR"


class OpticalAnomalyEngine:
    """Rolling-window anomaly detector for optical telemetry frames.

    Maintains a window of valid frames and computes statistical
    measures to detect channel anomalies.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        window_size: int = 100,
        intensity_anomaly_threshold: float = 3.0,  # std deviations
        disagreement_threshold: float = 0.15,
    ) -> None:
        self._window_size = window_size
        self._intensity_threshold = intensity_anomaly_threshold
        self._disagreement_threshold = disagreement_threshold

        # Rolling window data
        self._intensities: deque[float] = deque(maxlen=window_size)
        self._alice_bits: deque[Optional[int]] = deque(maxlen=window_size)
        self._alice_bases: deque[Optional[int]] = deque(maxlen=window_size)
        self._bob_bits: deque[Optional[int]] = deque(maxlen=window_size)
        self._bob_bases: deque[Optional[int]] = deque(maxlen=window_size)
        self._sequences: deque[int] = deque(maxlen=window_size)

        self._total_frames = 0
        self._valid_frames = 0
        self._invalid_frames = 0
        self._last_sequence: Optional[int] = None
        self._total_gaps = 0

    def ingest_frame(
        self,
        sequence: int,
        normalized_intensity: float,
        alice_basis: Optional[int] = None,
        alice_bit: Optional[int] = None,
        bob_basis: Optional[int] = None,
        bob_bit: Optional[int] = None,
        frame_valid: bool = True,
    ) -> None:
        """Ingest a validated telemetry frame into the rolling window."""
        self._total_frames += 1

        if not frame_valid:
            self._invalid_frames += 1
            return

        self._valid_frames += 1

        # Track sequence gaps
        if self._last_sequence is not None:
            gap = sequence - self._last_sequence - 1
            if gap > 0:
                self._total_gaps += gap
        self._last_sequence = sequence

        # Add to rolling window
        self._intensities.append(normalized_intensity)
        self._alice_bits.append(alice_bit)
        self._alice_bases.append(alice_basis)
        self._bob_bits.append(bob_bit)
        self._bob_bases.append(bob_basis)
        self._sequences.append(sequence)

    def analyze(self) -> AnomalyReport:
        """Analyze current window for anomalies."""
        n = len(self._intensities)
        if n == 0:
            return AnomalyReport()

        # Intensity statistics
        intensities = np.array(list(self._intensities))
        mean_i = float(np.mean(intensities))
        std_i = float(np.std(intensities)) if n > 1 else 0.0

        # Bit disagreement rate (all pairs)
        disagreements = 0
        compared = 0
        for i in range(n):
            if self._alice_bits[i] is not None and self._bob_bits[i] is not None:
                compared += 1
                if self._alice_bits[i] != self._bob_bits[i]:
                    disagreements += 1
        bit_disagreement = disagreements / compared if compared > 0 else 0.0

        # Basis-matched disagreement rate
        basis_disagreements = 0
        basis_compared = 0
        for i in range(n):
            if (self._alice_bits[i] is not None
                    and self._bob_bits[i] is not None
                    and self._alice_bases[i] is not None
                    and self._bob_bases[i] is not None
                    and self._alice_bases[i] == self._bob_bases[i]):
                basis_compared += 1
                if self._alice_bits[i] != self._bob_bits[i]:
                    basis_disagreements += 1
        basis_disagreement = basis_disagreements / basis_compared if basis_compared > 0 else 0.0

        # Frame loss rate
        frame_loss = self._invalid_frames / self._total_frames if self._total_frames > 0 else 0.0

        # Sequence gaps in window
        gaps = 0
        seqs = list(self._sequences)
        for i in range(1, len(seqs)):
            if seqs[i] - seqs[i - 1] > 1:
                gaps += seqs[i] - seqs[i - 1] - 1

        # Anomaly detection
        reasons = []
        anomaly = False

        if std_i > 0 and n >= 10:
            # Check for intensity anomalies (sudden changes)
            recent = intensities[-min(10, n):]
            recent_mean = float(np.mean(recent))
            if abs(recent_mean - mean_i) > self._intensity_threshold * std_i:
                anomaly = True
                reasons.append(
                    f"Intensity shift: recent_mean={recent_mean:.3f}, "
                    f"window_mean={mean_i:.3f}, std={std_i:.3f}"
                )

        if basis_disagreement > self._disagreement_threshold:
            anomaly = True
            reasons.append(
                f"High basis-matched disagreement: {basis_disagreement:.3f} "
                f"> threshold {self._disagreement_threshold:.3f}"
            )

        if frame_loss > 0.2:
            anomaly = True
            reasons.append(f"High frame loss rate: {frame_loss:.3f}")

        if gaps > n * 0.1:
            anomaly = True
            reasons.append(f"Excessive sequence gaps: {gaps} in window of {n}")

        return AnomalyReport(
            window_size=n,
            valid_frames=self._valid_frames,
            intensity_mean=round(mean_i, 4),
            intensity_std=round(std_i, 4),
            bit_disagreement_rate=round(bit_disagreement, 4),
            basis_matched_disagreement_rate=round(basis_disagreement, 4),
            frame_loss_rate=round(frame_loss, 4),
            sequence_gaps=gaps,
            anomaly_detected=anomaly,
            anomaly_reasons=reasons,
        )

    def reset(self) -> None:
        """Reset the anomaly engine."""
        self._intensities.clear()
        self._alice_bits.clear()
        self._alice_bases.clear()
        self._bob_bits.clear()
        self._bob_bases.clear()
        self._sequences.clear()
        self._total_frames = 0
        self._valid_frames = 0
        self._invalid_frames = 0
        self._last_sequence = None
        self._total_gaps = 0

results.description:
Explore Armos (QNu Labs Quantum Key Distribution System), its cryptographic mechanism, advantages, and importance in quantum-safe encryption systems.
Share # Armos (QNu Labs Quantum Key Distribution System)
What

Armos is QNu Labs' quantum key distribution product that makes encryption keys using the laws of physics instead of math. It works up to 150 kilometers over regular fiber optic cables. The physics is straightforward: we send single photons encoded with random bits. If someone tries to intercept them, quantum mechanics guarantees they disturb the signal in a way we can detect. When we see too many errors, we know someone's listening and we stop This gives you information-theoretic security - meaning no amount of computing power, now or ever, can break it. The Indian Army and Indian Navy use Armos to protect classified communications. You can buy it directly through the Government eMarketplace.
Why Data with 25-year sensitivity like medical records or state secrets needs protection that lasts, not just protection that's hard to break today.

Impact

Armos protects against "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks where adversaries store encrypted data today to decrypt it in 2030-2035 when quantum computers arrive.

For defense, banking, and government, this is the only way to guarantee long-term secrecy.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) uses quantum physics to securely distribute encryption keys. Armos (QKD) transmits keys using randomly generated photons over a fiber cable. It detects eavesdroppers, providing secure symmetric key distribution for encrypting confidential data ## How Armos - Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) achieves unconditional security?
Armos QKD enables to create secure encryption keys for any two ends of a communication link for Symmetric Key Encryption system without ever sharing the actual keys on any links #### Quantum Safe Networks
Terrestrial networks spanning agencies, states, or countries need end-to-end encryption for secure communication. Armos QKD enables a quantum-safe network, ensuring the highest level of data trust #### Transition to Secure Digital Key Transfer
Armos QKD offers quantum-safe key management for real-time confidential data transport across any network, transforming secure key distribution in defense and allied sectors for a strategic advantage #### End-to-End Encryption

You won't need a modem. Just a router. Modem's are only for MODulating/DEModulating the signals between different infrastructure mediums: translating a fiber or co-ax cable signal into an Ethernet or Wifi signal inside your home With Quantum/CL fiber, the modulating/demodulating is done at what's called the ONT (optical network terminal). ## Big picture in one breath

```text
Alice signs a message the quantum way
        ↓
a signature package is created
        ↓
Bob (and maybe Trent) verifies it
        ↓
ShorlyNot looks at the measurement numbers
        ↓
ACCEPT  or  REJECT + threat type
```

No ML. Just quantum steps + simple math thresholds.

---

## Step 0 — Setup (once, before signing)

1. System creates **entangled pairs** (Bell-type links).  
   Think: Alice and Bob each hold matching “quantum halves” that are correlated.

2. Those halves act like **quantum key material** for signatures  
   (not the same job as a normal password, but same idea: only the right parties have the right stuff).

3. Everyone gets IDs: `key_id`, who is Alice, who is Bob, etc.

4. Optional: classical messages (correction bits later) can be wrapped with **PQC** so a normal hacker can’t easily read/flip them.

After setup, the system is idle and green.

---

## Step 1 — Alice signs

Alice types a message (or a payment form).

What ShorlyNot does:

1. Turn message into **bits**
2. Encode bits into **quantum states** (Pauli eigenstates — basically “this bit is prepared this way on the Bloch axes”)
3. Use **teleportation-style** steps with the entangled pairs:
   - Alice does a Bell-type measurement
   - That produces **classical correction bits** (the Pauli correction info)
4. Bundle a **signature object**:

```text
signature = {
  message (or hash),
  measurement / quantum transcript,
  Pauli correction bits,
  nonce (one-time id),
  key_id,
  profile (e.g. teleport / arbiter),
  timestamp
}
```

5. That signature is what gets sent to Bob (over normal network as data the app understands; the “quantum” part was simulated/prepared in the engine).

**Important:** each honest sign should burn one-time material (nonce + key chunk) so the same signature can’t be freely reused forever.

---

## Step 2 — Bob verifies

Bob receives: message + signature.

What ShorlyNot does:

1. Check basic stuff first (fast, classical):
   - is `nonce` new? (not seen before)
   - does `key_id` match Alice?
   - is Bob allowed to verify this?
   - is signature format sane?

2. If those fail → **stop early**  
   - reused nonce → **REPLAY**  
   - wrong key / wrong person → **IMPERSONATION**  
   - not allowed → **UNAUTH_VERIFY**

3. If basics pass → **quantum verify path**:
   - apply **Pauli corrections** using the classical bits
   - do **projective measurements**
   - compare outcomes to what the message/encoding says should happen

4. Compute **mismatch rate**  
   (“out of N checks, how many disagreed?”)

5. Compare to threshold **τ**:
   - mismatch ≤ τ → **ACCEPT** (looks legitimate)
   - mismatch > τ → **REJECT** (looks forged or channel-broken)

τ is not vibes. It’s set from expected noise + a safety margin so honest noise doesn’t always trip the alarm, but random fakes usually do.

---

## Step 3 — Threat detection (always on top of verify)

Every verify produces numbers. The detector reads them and stamps a label.

| What it sees | Label |
|---|---|
| Clean, low mismatch, fresh nonce, right key | `OK` |
| Random/fake signature, high mismatch | `FORGERY` |
| Old signature sent again | `REPLAY` |
| Right-looking format, wrong quantum identity | `IMPERSONATION` |
| Someone verifying without permission | `UNAUTH_VERIFY` |
| Correction bits flipped / noise spike / weird histograms | `CHANNEL` |

Rules only. Like:

- if nonce in used-set → REPLAY  
- if key_id unbound → IMPERSONATION  
- if mismatch > τ → FORGERY or CHANNEL (depending on other signals)  
- if Pauli histogram looks nothing like honest encoding → FORGERY  

That’s the “cyber threat detection framework” the PS wants.

---

## Step 4 — What the user sees when it’s working

### Normal day
1. Alice hits **Sign**  
2. Bob hits **Verify**  
3. Screen goes **green ACCEPT**  
4. Mismatch is small (e.g. 1–3% from noise)  
5. Log line: `OK · 2.1 ms · mismatch 0.02 · τ 0.08`

### Attack day
Someone hits **Forge** (or a real attacker sends junk):

1. Verify runs  
2. Mismatch jumps (e.g. ~25–50%)  
3. Screen **red REJECT**  
4. Label **FORGERY**  
5. Metrics update: forge attempts detected, \(P_{\text{forge}}\) display  

Replay:
1. Same signature sent twice  
2. Second time dies on nonce check  
3. **REPLAY** even if quantum part would have looked fine  

So working system = **two layers**:
- quantum verify (does physics match?)  
- threat rules (is this a known dirty pattern?)

---

## Step 5 — Evaluation lab (also always there)

In the background / metrics tab the system can run many trials:

- 1000 honest signs → almost all accept  
- 1000 forgeries → almost all reject  
- estimate **forgery probability** (chance a faker slips through)  
- show false reject (honest rejected by mistake)  
- show latency  

That’s how you “evaluate the framework” like the PS says.

---

## Optional layers (platform, not the main loop)

These can sit around the same flow:

**QKD module**  
Sometimes used to make shared session keys for encrypting traffic or protecting classical channels — side feature.

**PQC module**  
Wraps the classical Pauli correction bits so flipping them mid-wire is harder.

**Edge/modem (later)**  
Control PC does heavy quantum sim.  
A light box only checks the **signature transcript** + thresholds + “block/alert”.  
Same logic, weaker machine.

Ignore hardware for now: on a laptop, control plane does everything.

---

## Full lifecycle of one message

```text
1. SETUP
   entangled key material ready
   Alice, Bob registered

2. SIGN (Alice)
   message → quantum encode → teleport-style sign
   → signature package + nonce

3. SEND
   message + signature to Bob
   (correction bits optionally PQC-protected)

4. VERIFY (Bob)
   classical checks (nonce, identity, permission)
   → quantum corrections + measurements
   → mismatch vs τ

5. DETECT
   rules stamp OK or threat type

6. RESULT
   ACCEPT or REJECT
   log + metrics updated

7. CONSUME
   nonce / one-time key chunk marked used
   (replay next time will fail)
```

That’s the whole engine, looping every time someone signs.

---

## Mental model (simplest)

Think of a **wax seal**, but quantum:

1. Alice melts the seal in a special way only her entangled material allows  
2. Bob checks if the seal pattern matches the letter  
3. ShorlyNot also checks:  
   - is this seal photocopied from yesterday? (replay)  
   - is it a random blob? (forgery)  
   - is it someone else’s seal? (impersonation)  
   - did someone smudge it in transit? (channel)  

Working product = that loop, live, with numbers, every click.

---

## What “working” means in practice

You can sit down and:

1. Sign a real-looking message → always (or almost always) accepted  
2. Press forge → rejected and labeled  
3. Press replay → rejected  
4. Press impersonate → rejected  
5. See a graph that forgeries get harder as you use more quantum material  
6. See verify finish in milliseconds for normal sizes  

If those six things happen, **the project is working** — as a whole system, not as scattered quantum demos.

---

That’s the general working picture: **setup → sign → verify → threshold detect → accept/reject + logs/metrics**, repeat.

# PRD — ShorlyNot (SIH 2026 · PS 26141)

**Product:** ShorlyNot  
**Problem statement:** 26141 — Quantum-Inspired Cyber Threat Detection for Digital Signature Security  
**Org theme:** Blockchain & Cybersecurity · Egreen Quanta  
**Document status:** v1.0 — build start point  
**Date:** 2026-08-30  

---

## 1. One-line vision

ShorlyNot is a **quantum security infrastructure (skeleton)** plus a **mock banking application** built on top of it: every sensitive bank action is protected by **QDS + QKD + PQC**, threats are detected with **non-ML statistical thresholds**, and a **SOC dashboard** can **lock the bank** when attacks escalate.

---

## 2. Problem we solve (PS 26141)

Classical public-key signatures (RSA/ECC) are threatened by Shor’s algorithm.  
PS 26141 asks for a **quantum-inspired cyber threat detection framework** for **teleportation-based Quantum Digital Signature (QDS)** systems that:

- Detects **forgery, impersonation, replay, unauthorized verification** (and channel manipulation)
- Uses **Pauli eigenstates, projective measurements, statistical thresholds** — **no AI/ML**
- Keeps **efficient verification** and **information-theoretic security framing**
- Is evaluated via **forgery probability, attack simulations, performance metrics**

**ShorlyNot answer:**  
Implement that framework as a reusable **skeleton**, then prove it with a **bank mock app** where attacks have visible product consequences (lockdown).

---

## 3. Product structure (exactly two deliverables)

| # | Name | Role |
|---|------|------|
| **A** | `skeleton/` | **Infra / framework** — QKD + PQC + QDS + detect + stages + metrics. Show judges the invention. Embed-anywhere. |
| **B** | `bank/` | **Application built on skeleton** — mock bank UI + background SOC. Shows the engine in a real-looking product. Can full-lock. |

```text
legacy/   ← old fintech, Coms, finquantum-shield, shorlynot (source of reusable methods only)
skeleton/ ← THE framework (single brain)
bank/     ← THE app (calls skeleton only; no duplicate quantum logic)
```

**Hard rule:** Bank never reimplements QDS/QKD/PQC/detect. It only **consumes** skeleton APIs/SDK.

---

## 4. Goals

### 4.1 Primary (must win PS)

1. Teleportation-based **QDS** sign + verify (Pauli eigenstates, corrections, projective measurements)
2. **Threat detection framework** (threshold / statistical — no ML):
   - Forgery  
   - Impersonation  
   - Replay  
   - Unauthorized verification  
   - Channel manipulation  
3. **Forgery probability analysis**, attack simulations, performance metrics  
4. Clear **mathematical/model docs** + **delivery table** mapping PS → code  
5. Demo path a judge understands in ≤ 3 minutes  

### 4.2 Product goals

6. Mock bank that feels like a normal bank (not a full real-world bank clone)
7. SOC dashboard showing pipeline, threats, stages, metrics; quantum engine “in the background” of customer UI  
8. **Lock ladder** that freezes bank operations when threats escalate (iptables-era enforcement *idea*, app-level now)  
9. Skeleton usable standalone (CLI + API) to prove embeddability  

### 4.3 Platform goals

10. **QKD + PQC + QDS** all real layers (not optional classical-only mode)  
11. **SIM** and **IBM Quantum API** backends  
12. **Qiskit** primary in bank path; **PennyLane** primary in skeleton (fallback if missing) — not both engines on every request  

---

## 5. Non-goals (explicit freeze)

- Full commercial core-banking (loans, cards, KYC, UPI rails, etc.)
- ML/AI detection models  
- Modem/OpenWrt firmware as a build blocker (stub OK; hardware later)  
- Claiming equivalence to commercial QKD appliances (e.g. Armos)  
- Running IBM on every UI click (queues break demos)  
- Four parallel root products  
- Quantum engine optional / bypass for “happy path” demo  

---

## 6. Users & personas

| Persona | Needs |
|---------|--------|
| **Customer (alice/bob/carol)** | Login, see balances, transfer, history; see lock message if frozen |
| **Attacker (eve)** | Judge-ready attack flow against live transfer signatures / session |
| **Operator (SOC)** | Watch events, stages, metrics, force review, observe lockdown |
| **Judge / integrator** | Skeleton naked demo + bank proof app + docs/citations |
| **Developer** | Clean SDK: sign, verify, detect, metrics |

**Seeded accounts (demo):**

- `alice` / `bob` / `carol` — legitimate customers  
- `eve` — attacker flow  
- `ops` — SOC operator (optional same admin)

---

## 7. Core concepts

### 7.1 Layers (all always-on)

| Layer | Job |
|-------|-----|
| **QDS** | Sign & verify **transaction authenticity** (PS heart). Teleportation-based simulation/protocol path. |
| **QKD** | Session/link key material + link health (QBER). Supports platform; does **not** replace QDS. |
| **PQC** | Protect classical correction bits / hybrid recovery (e.g. ML-KEM-class). |
| **Detect (Q-STDF)** | Non-ML threshold engine on verification transcripts + link signals → threat labels. |
| **Stages + Enforce** | Map threats → S-stages (and secondary Q-stages) → bank lock actions. |

### 7.2 Signature object (conceptual)

```text
SignatureBundle:
  payload_hash          # hash of canonical transaction
  key_id                # signer binding
  nonce                 # one-time / replay stop
  profile               # e.g. qds_teleport | qds_arbiter
  correction_bits[]     # classical Pauli corrections (optionally PQC-wrapped)
  measurement_transcript[]
  backend               # sim | ibm
  engine                # qiskit | pennylane
  timestamp
```

### 7.3 Threat labels

`OK | FORGERY | IMPERSONATION | REPLAY | UNAUTH_VERIFY | CHANNEL`

### 7.4 Stage ladders

**Signature ladder (primary → bank lock):**

| Stage | Trigger (examples) | Bank effect |
|-------|--------------------|-------------|
| S0 | Clean QDS verifies | Full service |
| S1 | Soft mismatch / elevated noise | SOC warn only |
| S2 | FORGERY or IMPERSONATION | Block **new transfers** |
| S3 | REPLAY / UNAUTH_VERIFY patterns | Read-only / kill sessions |
| S4 | Repeated critical / CHANNEL storm | **FULL BANK LOCK** |

**QKD ladder (secondary → SOC; may assist lock at high levels):**

| Stage | Trigger | Effect |
|-------|---------|--------|
| Q0–Q2 | Normal → elevated QBER | SOC indicators |
| Q3–Q4 | Compromise-level QBER | Can push toward S3/S4 **with** policy; never sole “we solved 26141” story |

**Rule:** Signature threats alone must be able to fully lock the bank.

### 7.5 Backends

| Mode | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `sim` | Local Aer / PennyLane simulator (default demo) |
| `ibm` | IBM Quantum API when token present (lab / proof) |

UI **must** display active backend. No silent fake-hardware.

Quantum protocol path is **never skipped** — only the compute backend changes.

---

## 8. User journeys

### 8.1 Honest transfer (happy path)

1. Alice logs into bank mock  
2. Creates transfer to Bob  
3. Skeleton: QKD session check (support) → QDS sign → PQC-wrap corrections → QDS verify → detect OK  
4. Ledger posts; history shows success  
5. SOC shows S0, OK event, low mismatch  

### 8.2 Attacker flow (judge path)

1. Honest transfer once (baseline green)  
2. Eve runs attack (forge / replay / impersonate / unauth verify / channel) against **real transfer signature path**  
3. Detect returns threat label; stages climb  
4. At S2+ transfers blocked; at S4 bank locked  
5. Alice retry → clear “Security lock” bank message  
6. SOC shows metrics + threat feed  

### 8.3 Skeleton-only path

1. Operator runs skeleton CLI/API  
2. sign → verify → attack suite → metrics / P_forge  
3. No bank UI; proves embeddable infra  

---

## 9. Functional requirements

### 9.1 Skeleton

| ID | Requirement |
|----|-------------|
| SK-01 | QDS setup (entangled resource / key material abstraction) |
| SK-02 | QDS sign(payload) → SignatureBundle |
| SK-03 | QDS verify(payload, signature, verifier_ctx) → Accept/Reject + stats |

| SK-15 | engines: PennyLane primary; Qiskit fallback |
| SK-16 | CLI + HTTP API |
| SK-17 | pytest covering honest accept + each threat |
| SK-18 | docs: MODEL, REFERENCES (arXiv), DELIVERY_TABLE, BENCHMARKS |

### 9.2 Bank

| ID | Requirement |
|----|-------------|
| BK-01 | Mock bank UI: login, dashboard/balances, transfer, history, lock screen |
| BK-02 | Seeded users alice/bob/carol/eve |
| BK-03 | Ledger (balances + transactions) |
| BK-04 | Every transfer goes through skeleton (no bypass) |

### 9.3 Repo / quality

| RQ-01 | Root advertises only skeleton + bank |
| RQ-02 | legacy/ holds old trees |
| RQ-03 | No ML detection deps |
| RQ-04 | Honest claims only |

---

## 10. Non-functional requirements

| Area | Target |

| Verify latency (sim, n≈128) | Prefer < 100–500 ms on laptop for demo snappiness |
| Complexity story | Verification path O(n) on transcript stats; heavy circuit work behind sign/sim |

| Security framing | ITS **motivation under stated model**; publish measured rates; no “unbreakable” |

## 1. Official problem statement (summary)

### 1.1 Background (from PS)

- Quantum computing (e.g. Shor’s algorithm) threatens classical public-key systems (**RSA, ECC**).
- **Quantum Digital Signatures (QDS)** offer information-theoretic security using quantum mechanics.
- **Teleportation-based QDS** is promising for signature generation/verification via teleportation and entanglement.

### 1.2 Problem focus (from PS)

Build a **quantum-inspired cyber threat detection framework** for **QDS systems** that detects threats to integrity/authenticity of digital signatures:

- Forgery  
- Impersonation  
- Replay attacks  
- Unauthorized verification attempts  
- (and related) quantum channel manipulation  

**Without AI/ML.** Instead use:

- Pauli eigenstates  
- Projective measurements  
- Statistical analysis of measurement outcomes  
- Threshold-based decision rules  

while preserving information-theoretic security guarantees (as framing under a stated model).

### 1.3 Objectives (from PS)

1. Design a quantum-inspired threat detection framework for **teleportation-based QDS** protocols.  
2. Detect forgery, impersonation, replay, unauthorized verification.  
3. Use Pauli eigenstates, quantum measurement analysis, statistical thresholds.  
4. Efficient verification algorithms with ITS framing.  
5. Evaluate via forgery probability analysis, attack simulations, performance metrics.

### 1.4 Expected solution (from PS)

A **software framework** that:

- Simulates quantum public-key distribution using Bell-state entanglement and quantum teleportation  
- Applies Pauli correction operations and projective measurements for signature verification  
- Detects malicious activity via statistical evaluation and threshold rules  
- Includes mathematical modelling, attack simulation, security analysis, performance evaluation  
- Ensures deterministic acceptance of legitimate signatures (under ideal/stated conditions), low computational complexity, strong security guarantees  

---

## 2. Our solution — one paragraph

**ShorlyNot** is a software platform with **exactly two deliverables**:

2. **`bank/`** — a **mock banking application** built **on top of the skeleton** (no duplicate crypto brain). Customers use a normal-looking bank (login, balances, transfer, history). Every sensitive transfer is signed/verified by the skeleton. A background **SOC dashboard** shows threats and stages. When signature threats escalate, the **bank locks at application level** (not iptables).

**Simulation is the default quantum backend; IBM Quantum API is an optional real-hardware path.** Quantum processing is **never optional** — only the backend (`sim` | `ibm`) changes.

## 8. Functional specification — how software works

### 8.1 End-to-end happy path (bank transfer)

```text
1. Customer opens mock bank, logs in as alice
2. alice submits transfer → bob, amount X
3. Bank checks: session valid? bank not locked? balance enough?
4. Bank builds canonical transaction payload
5. Bank calls skeleton pipeline (no local crypto reimplementation)
6. Skeleton QKD: ensure session; record qber (support)
7. Skeleton QDS SIGN:
   - hash canonical payload
   - encode bits as Pauli eigenstates
   - entanglement / teleportation-style protocol
   - emit SignatureBundle (transcript, correction bits, nonce, key_id, …)
8. Skeleton PQC: protect classical correction bits
9. Skeleton QDS VERIFY:
   - unprotect corrections if needed
   - apply Pauli corrections
   - projective measurements
   - compute mismatch rate
   - compare to threshold τ
10. Skeleton Q-STDF detect:
   - classical binding: nonce fresh? key_id bound? authz OK?
   - quantum stats: mismatch vs τ; optional histogram checks
   - emit threat label OK | FORGERY | …
11. Skeleton stages: update S* (and Q* from qber)
12. If OK and stage allows: bank commits ledger (debit/credit), shows success
13. SOC logs event: OK, S0, mismatch, latency, backend
```

### 8.2 Attack path (judge demo)

```text
1. Complete one honest transfer (baseline green)
2. eve triggers attack against signature path:
   - FORGERY: fabricated / random signature or altered payload+bad sig
   - REPLAY: reuse prior SignatureBundle/nonce on new or same tx
   - IMPERSONATION: wrong key_id / missing signer material
   - UNAUTH_VERIFY: verify without authorization context
   - CHANNEL: flip/corrupt correction bits or transcript; noise blast
3. Q-STDF returns non-OK label
4. Stages escalate S0 → S2/S3/S4 per policy
5. Bank enforce:
   - S2: block new transfers
   - S3: read-only / invalidate sessions
   - S4: full bank lock banner
6. alice retry transfer → clear business error (“Security lock”)
7. SOC shows threat feed + metrics; optional P_forge panel
```

### 8.3 Skeleton-only path (infra demo)

```text
CLI/API without bank UI:
  setup → sign → verify → attack suite → metrics/bench
Proves embeddability and PS core without fintech chrome.
```

### 8.4 Pipeline contract (normative)

```text
pipeline.transfer_protect_sign_verify_detect(payload, ctx) →
  {
    accepted: bool,
    threat: OK|FORGERY|IMPERSONATION|REPLAY|UNAUTH_VERIFY|CHANNEL,
    mismatch: float,
    tau: float,
    stage_s: int,
    stage_q: int,
    signature: SignatureBundle | null,

  }
```

This is a genuinely strong PRD. Here's my honest, detailed take.

What's working really well

**The PS alignment is surgical.** Sections 23, 26, and the delivery table map every PS keyword to a code path. That's exactly how you win with technical judges. Most SIH teams describe their idea loosely — you've operationalized the fit.

**The two-product structure is smart.** `skeleton/` satisfies the technical evaluators, `bank/` gives non-technical judges a story they can follow. The "single brain" rule keeps them from diverging and becoming inconsistent, which kills many hackathon demos.

**The claims policy (Section 13) is mature.** Explicitly listing what you *cannot* say is rare and will protect you. SIH evaluators have seen enough teams claim "unbreakable quantum security" — your honesty will stand out.

**The Q-STDF naming is good.** Giving the detector its own name and acronym makes it feel like a real deliverable, not just `if mismatch > tau: reject`. That framing matters for judges.

**Section 23D (one-question fit test) is the sharpest line in the whole doc.** Keep it front and center. That's your north star for every build decision.

Real risks you need to address

**1. QDS implementation depth — this is your biggest technical risk.** The PRD says "teleportation-style protocol" but the actual quantum channel fidelity of your simulation will be scrutinized by any judge who knows QDS. You need to actually encode bits into Pauli eigenstates `|0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩, |−⟩`, entangle the signer-verifier channel, teleport the signature state, and apply Pauli corrections `{I, X, Z, XZ}` before projective measurement. If it's a classical mock that just returns plausible-looking mismatch numbers, a technical judge will catch it. PennyLane can do this properly — but the protocol needs to actually hold.

**2. The τ math needs to be real, not decorative.** You reference Hoeffding in 9.6, which is correct. A Hoeffding bound on measurement outcomes gives you: `τ = p₀ + sqrt(ln(1/δ) / 2n)` where n is the number of test measurements and δ is your desired false-reject probability. If you just hardcode 0.1 and 0.2 as "strict" and "lenient", that won't hold under scrutiny. Derive it, put it in MODEL.md with actual numbers, and display it in the SOC.

**3. Dual engine (PennyLane + Qiskit) is scope risk.** A shared `SignatureBundle` / `VerifyResult` contract across two quantum frameworks is real engineering work. If you're short on time, this is the first thing that will slip and cause bugs. I'd recommend PennyLane as the primary path and Qiskit as a clearly-deferred bonus, not an "alternate" you have to maintain in parallel.

**4. The bank UI ambiguity will bite you.** "React/Vite *or* polished HTML/CSS mock" — commit to one now. If you go React, lock the component library today. If general judges are your bank's audience, the UI matters more than you might think. A Streamlit SOC and a half-built React bank is a common SIH failure mode.

**5. PQC/ML-KEM is honest-but-thin as written.** The `else documented wrapper + stable interface` fallback is the right move, but make sure the fallback isn't invisible to judges. If ML-KEM doesn't make it in, have a visible `pqc.py` that clearly wraps ECDH or AES-GCM with a comment saying "ML-KEM interface stub — production would swap here." Judges respect an honest stub more than pretending.

What's missing from the PRD

- **Team composition and roles** — who owns skeleton vs bank vs UI? This matters for execution against the phase plan.
- **Actual timeline dates** — Phase P0–P8 needs dates, not just sequence. SIH internal deadline is likely December 2026.
- **The MODEL.md math is referenced everywhere but doesn't exist yet** — write at least the skeleton (τ derivation, Pauli correction table, protocol steps) before you start coding. It will force clarity.
- **Multiparty/arbiter (Trent) handling** — PS 26141's teleportation-based QDS literature typically involves three parties (Signer, Verifier, Arbitrator). You've deferred this, which is fine for MVP, but make sure two-party QDS is explicitly motivated in the docs or judges will flag it.

Tactical recommendations

**Build in this order, strict:** QDS sign → QDS verify (honest path) → Q-STDF detect (forgery first) → stages → attacks → pipeline → bank transfer (one endpoint) → SOC → bank lock → everything else. If you get through QDS verify and Q-STDF forgery detection with working tests, you've already won PS 26141 technically.

**The SOC dashboard is your presentation secret weapon.** Dark theme, live mismatch vs τ chart, stage indicator, threat label in red — that visual is what judges will photograph. Invest time here proportional to its demo impact.

**Run the Section 23D test every two weeks.** If at any point you can't demo "forge → caught → bank locks" in under 2 minutes, stop and fix it before adding features.

Bottom line

This is one of the best-structured SIH PRDs I've seen — clear PS fit, honest claims, clean architecture, realistic risk management. The danger is that you've defined an ambitious system and the implementation quality of the QDS core will determine whether you win or just look good on paper. The math and the quantum protocol need to actually be there, not simulated with random numbers wearing quantum clothes.

What is Missing — Categorized
CRITICAL (will block the build or sink the demo)

1. No QDS protocol variant named
The PRD says "teleportation-based QDS" everywhere but never says which paper you're implementing. There are multiple variants — Dunjko-Wallden-Andersson (2014), Lu et al. (2015), the Yin et al. streamlined scheme. Each has different state preparation steps, different numbers of test qubits, different Pauli correction logic. Until you pick one and name it, your qds/ module has no ground truth to implement against. This is the single biggest gap.

2. MODEL.md doesn't exist
It's referenced 6+ times but it's empty. It needs to contain at minimum:

The Pauli eigenstate encoding table (which bit maps to which state)
The teleportation channel step-by-step
The Pauli correction lookup {00→I, 01→X, 10→Z, 11→XZ}
The τ derivation (Hoeffding formula with actual numbers)
The forgery probability formula P_forge as a function of n and key length

Without this, two developers on your team will implement two different things.

3. No timeline with actual dates
Phase P0 through P8 are in the right sequence but there are zero dates. SIH internal deadlines exist. Without dates, this is a wish list. You need to know what week you need QDS tests passing vs what week bank UI starts.

4. No team composition or role assignment
The PRD doesn't say who owns what. Skeleton is a full-stack quantum engineering job. Bank is a full-stack web job. SOC is a frontend job. These can't all be one person. Who is the quantum lead? Who owns the React/bank UI? Who owns the FastAPI layer? Without this, everything becomes everyone's problem and nothing gets done.

SIGNIFICANT (will cause quality or credibility gaps)

5. τ formula not derived
You mention "Hoeffding-inspired" in section 9.6 but the actual formula isn't written. For a PS that explicitly says "statistical threshold methods," judges will ask you to explain your threshold. The formula is: τ = p₀ + √(ln(1/δ) / 2n). Write it in MODEL.md, define p₀ (honest noise floor), n (number of test measurements per signature), and δ (target false-reject probability). Then back-calculate what n needs to be for reasonable δ.

6. No specification of signature length / test qubit count
How many qubits constitute one signature? How many test states? How many verification measurements? This determines your circuit size, your simulation latency, and your forgery probability formula. It needs a number. Even a reasonable default like "n = 100 test qubits per signature, security parameter l = 128" is enough.

7. Bank UI decision not made
"React/Vite or polished HTML/CSS mock" — this ambiguity will cause scope confusion mid-build. Pick one today. If anyone on the team knows React, use it — the SOC dashboard will look significantly better with a proper component library. If not, committed clean HTML/CSS is better than half-built React.

8. No wireframes or mockups for the bank or SOC
The customer bank has 5 pages listed. The SOC has 6 required panels. Nothing is drawn. Before a single line of frontend code, someone needs to sketch what these look like — even on paper. The SOC especially needs to be planned because it needs to show mismatch vs τ, stage indicator, threat feed, and metrics simultaneously without looking like a mess.

9. Legacy code audit is absent
Section 5 says "park under legacy/" but doesn't say what's actually salvageable. Your existing QKD/BB84 patterns, dashboard UX, and escalation logic are all reuse candidates. Without an audit, you'll waste time rebuilding things that exist or worse, accidentally copy in bad patterns.

MODERATE (will matter for final polish)

10. REFERENCES.md is empty
The papers you're building on need to be listed. At minimum: the QDS paper you're implementing, the Hoeffding bound paper, the PQC standard you're using. Judges who ask "which paper is your protocol based on?" and get "uh, some arXiv thing" will mark you down. Takes one hour to write.

11. PQC decision is unresolved
"ML-KEM if feasible, else honest strong wrapper" — this needs to be decided before P3. ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber / FIPS 203) is in pqcrypto pip packages. It works. Either commit to it or commit to "AES-256-GCM with documented ML-KEM-ready interface." The ambiguity will slow the P3 phase.

12. No error handling strategy
What happens when PennyLane throws an exception mid-signature? What does the bank show? What does the SOC log? This isn't just robustness — it's demo safety. The worst thing during a live demo is an unhandled exception crashing the transfer page in front of judges.

13. No seeded data specification
alice, bob, carol, eve are named but there's no spec for: starting balances, which accounts can transfer to which, what eve's attack permissions are, what the demo transaction amounts are. This needs a seed.py or fixture file spec.

14. No demo day deployment plan
Will this run on one laptop? Two? A hosted server? What's the URL judges hit? What happens if the laptop dies? These are not PRD-level concerns normally but for a SIH demo they absolutely are. You need a DEPLOY.md that says "runs on one machine, ports X and Y, start with this command."

The 0.5 points holding you back from 8

The gap between 7.5 and 8 is one thing: the QDS protocol is described architecturally but not scientifically. Once you name the paper, write the Pauli table, and derive τ — the PRD becomes genuinely build-ready. Right now it's strategically excellent but technically underspecified at the quantum layer, which is ironically the most important layer for PS 26141.

Everything else is execution hygiene. The strategic thinking is already top tier for SIH.

Petros Wallden^1,2,*, Vedran Dunjko^3,4,5, Adrian Kent^6,7, and Erika Andersson^2 ## Abstract
Digital signatures guarantee the authenticity and transferability of messages and are widely used in modern communication. # A QDS scheme based on superdense teleportation
## Abstract
Quantum digital signature is a basic cryptographic primitive with extensive application, such as e-commerce and e-government. In this paper, we propose a quantum digital signature scheme of 2-bit messages based on the idea of superdense teleportation. In our scheme, the sender randomly generates a quantum signature by applying some unitary transformations on her registers and measuring them with Bell basis, and the receivers verify the quantum signature by applying some unitary transformations on their registers and measuring them with computational basis Since the sender’s measurement result, which is randomly obtained, partially determines the public key and thus participates the receivers’ verification, no arbitrator is required. By quantum mechanics, we also show that our scheme of 2-bit messages is unconditionally secure. In addition, our scheme can be used to securely sign multi-bit messages by simple iteration ## References

# Improving BB84 Efficiency with Delayed Measurement via Quantum Memory
###### Abstract
In this paper, we introduce a novel modification to the BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol, aimed at enhancing its efficiency through the use of quantum memory and delayed measurement. In the standard BB84 protocol, the receiver immediately measures the qubits sent by the sender using randomly chosen bases. Due to mismatches between the sender and receiver’s bases, a significant portion of the qubits are discarded, reducing the overall key generation rate Our proposed protocol allows the receiver to store the received qubits in quantum memory and defer measurement until after the sender reveals her basis choices, effectively eliminating the need to discard mismatched qubits This modification improves the key generation efficiency while maintaining the core security features of the standard BB84 protocol. By avoiding the unnecessary loss of qubits, our protocol achieves a higher secret key rate without introducing additional vulnerabilities. We present a detailed step-by-step explanation of the delayed measurement process. Although this approach does not alter the security guarantees of BB84, it represents a significant improvement in efficiency, making the protocol more viable for large-scale quantum communication networks ## 1 Introduction
In this paper, we propose a modification to the BB84 protocol that leverages quantum memory and delayed measurement to address this inefficiency. The receiver stores qubits upon receipt rather than measuring them immediately, and measures them only after receiving the sender’s basis information. This modification eliminates the need to discard mismatched qubits, increasing the efficiency and overall key generation rate while maintaining the security guarantees of the original protocol ## 3 Proposed Protocol
In the modified BB84 protocol, the sender transmits qubits as in the original BB84 protocol, using randomly chosen bases. However, instead of immediately measuring the qubits upon receipt, the receiver stores them in a quantum memory. After the transmission of all qubits, the sender communicates the basis used for each qubit through a classical channel. The receiver then measures the stored qubits using the correct basis, thus eliminating the need to discard qubits due to mismatches ### 3.1   BB84 Scenario

In this paper, we have proposed a novel modification to the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol that leverages quantum memory to delay the measurement of qubits until after the basis information has been shared. This approach effectively eliminates the need to discard qubits due to basis mismatches, thereby significantly increasing the key generation rate while preserving the fundamental security properties of the original BB84 protocol Our security analysis demonstrates that the modified protocol maintains robustness against eavesdropping attempts, as it adheres to the core quantum mechanical principles that underlie the security of BB84, including the no-cloning theorem and the measurement disturbance phenomenon. ## I Introduction
The first QDS protocol, proposed by Gottesman and Chuang [2], required involved processing of the quantum signatures – a general SWAP test and long-term quantum memory – which is currently unfeasible experimentally. In [3], an optical multiport replaced the SWAP test. Long-term quantum memory was however still required. ![CI](https://github.com/Sansyuh06/yessit2026-Shorly_Not/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)

**Quantum-Safe Communication, Secured by Physics.**

# ShorlyNot: Quantum-Key-Bound Network Lease Enforcement Platform

SHORLYNOT is a quantum-aware network authorization and enforcement platform.
The core security primitive is the Quantum-Key-Bound Network Lease (QKBNL), which binds physical quantum key distribution security guarantees to localized router-level firewall enforcement.

## Features
- **Quantum Backends**: Supports Qiskit simulation (Aer) and real IBM Quantum Hardware execution.
- **Protocols**: BB84, B92, E91, Decoy-State BB84.
- **Physical Enforcement**: Dynamic iptables/OpenWRT firewall enforcement.
- **Security Event Monitoring**: Real-time detection of QBER threshold violations.
- **PQC Recovery**: Automated Post-Quantum Cryptography (ML-KEM-768) handshake for lease restoration during channel compromise.

## Execution Modes

SHORLYNOT supports three core execution modes. Set `SHORLYNOT_EXECUTION_MODE` in your `.env`.

### 1. SIMULATION
* `SHORLYNOT_EXECUTION_MODE=simulation`
* Uses local Qiskit Aer for quantum circuit execution.
* Uses mock/simulated interfaces for Arduino serial telemetry and Router enforcement.
* This is the default mode for development and local UI testing.

### 2. REAL
* `SHORLYNOT_EXECUTION_MODE=real`
* **Requires**: `IBM_QUANTUM_TOKEN` for real quantum execution.
* **Requires**: Real OpenWRT/Linux router API connection.
* **Requires**: Real Arduino serial connection for optical telemetry.
* Executes actual circuits on IBM hardware and manipulates live firewall rules.

### 3. REPLAY
* `SHORLYNOT_EXECUTION_MODE=replay`
* Uses previously stored immutable evidence records to replay a past execution sequence.

# Quantum-Aware Secure Chat (BB84 Demo)

## What this project is
Two people chat securely over Wi-Fi through a normal home router.
Instead of RSA/ECDH, a lightweight BB84-style simulator generates shared secrets.
The system watches quantum-link health (QBER) and reacts to attacks by rotating ports/IPs,
then escalating to network changes or lockdown. This shows how networks can become
"quantum-aware" without replacing existing hardware.

## Repo layout
- quantum_engine/bb84_simulator.py - BB84 simulator with QBER + attack detection
- kms/key_management_service.py - KMS core logic and escalation tracking
- kms/kms_server.py - FastAPI server + status UI
- chat/chat_server.py - WebSocket relay (no decryption)
- chat/client_app.py - Terminal client with AES-256-GCM
- chat/client_gui.py - Tkinter GUI client with AES-256-GCM
- router/router_guard.sh - Router guard script (OpenWrt-style simulation)

## Setup
1. Install dependencies:
   python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

2. Configure IPs
   Example LAN:
   - Router: 192.168.1.1
   - Laptop (KMS + chat server): 192.168.1.100

   If your LAN uses different addresses, update:
   - router/router_guard.sh (KMS_HOST, PRIMARY_IP, BACKUP_IP)
   - chat/client_app.py defaults (KMS base URL, WS URL) or enter them at runtime.

## Run (demo sequence)
1. Start KMS (API + status UI):
   python -m kms.kms_server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

   Status UI: http://192.168.1.100:8000/

2. Start chat relay:
   python -m chat.chat_server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765

3. Start router guard (Linux/OpenWrt box or VM):
   sh router/router_guard.sh

   Note: The script uses iptables and may require root privileges.
   It simulates port/IP/network escalation; IP changes are logged and conceptual.

4. Start two clients (Alice and Bob):
   python -m chat.client_app
   python -m chat.client_app

## One-command launcher
Start KMS, chat server, and two GUI clients:
python start_all.py

Options:
- --no-gui (skip GUI clients)
- --clients N (number of GUI windows to open)

## GUI chat client (optional)
If you prefer a GUI, run:
python -m chat.client_gui

## Normal GREEN demo
1. Create a new session (client will call /create_session).
2. Chat normally. QBER should be low and status stays GREEN.
3. Use /status inside the client to view link health.

## Trigger Eve / attack demo
Option A (UI): click Activate Eve or Trigger Attack at http://192.168.1.100:8000/
Option B (CLI):
- Activate Eve: curl -X POST http://192.168.1.100:8000/activate_eve
- Trigger attack: curl -X POST http://192.168.1.100:8000/trigger_attack

Expected behavior:
- QBER rises toward 20-30%.

## 1. Executive Summary

**ShorlyNot** is a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) simulation system that enables two legitimate parties (Alice and Bob) to securely establish a shared secret key while detecting the presence of an eavesdropper (Eve) through quantum measurement-induced errors.

### What Makes This Project Different

Unlike most QKD demonstrations that use pseudo-random number generators to *pretend* to simulate quantum mechanics, ShorlyNot uses **real Qiskit `QuantumCircuit` objects** running on the **AerSimulator** — IBM's quantum circuit simulator. This means:

- **QBER (Quantum Bit Error Rate)** emerges from actual quantum measurement statistics
- The 25% error rate from Eve is not hardcoded — it is a **physical consequence** of the no-cloning theorem
- The system uses real quantum gates (X, H, measurement) on real qubit circuits
- Privacy amplification, key derivation, and encryption follow published standards

### Key Capabilities

| Capability | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| BB84 QKD Protocol | Real Qiskit quantum circuits for key generation |
| Eavesdropper Detection | QBER-based detection with 11% Shor-Preskill threshold |
| Privacy Amplification | Toeplitz matrix hashing to remove Eve's partial information |
| Key Derivation | HKDF-SHA256 to produce uniform 256-bit AES keys |
| Encryption | AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption |
| Escalation FSM | 4-level automated defense (port → IP → network → lockdown) |
| Real-time Dashboard | Streamlit + Plotly monitoring with live QBER chart |
| Attacker Console | Interactive Rich TUI for demonstrating attacks |
| Event Logger | WebSocket-powered real-time event feed |

---

## 2. Problem Statement & Motivation

### The Threat: Quantum Computers vs Current Encryption

Most encryption today relies on **computational hardness assumptions**:

| Algorithm | What It Protects | Quantum Threat |
|-----------|-----------------|----------------|
| RSA-2048 | Key exchange, digital signatures | **Broken** by Shor's algorithm |
| ECC (P-256) | Key exchange, signatures | **Broken** by Shor's algorithm |
| AES-256 | Symmetric encryption | Weakened by Grover's (AES-128 equivalent) |

The threat model is called **"Harvest Now, Decrypt Later"** — adversaries are already collecting encrypted traffic today, waiting for quantum computers powerful enough to decrypt it.

### The Solution: Quantum Key Distribution

QKD uses the **laws of quantum physics** (not mathematical assumptions) to secure communication:

- **No-cloning theorem:** An eavesdropper cannot copy unknown quantum states
- **Measurement disturbance:** Measuring a quantum state irreversibly changes it
- **Information-theoretic security:** Secure even against adversaries with unlimited computational power
